dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read both next-shims.d.ts files, fixture vite/next configs, pages, and grepped the next/* import surface across both apps — genuine contract enumeration from the fixtures.
Wrote all next/* shims as self-described 'quick stubs'/'very minimal versions' from memory rather than grounding each in the type signatures it had just read.
Only ls'd /opt/reference/node_modules and read one package.json; never opened the Vite plugin API .d.ts types.

Ambiguous params-Promise semantics resolved by reasoning from Next.js memory ('In Next.js 15+ params are always Promise'); said 'let me check the actual Next.js 16 signature' but never consulted vendored source.
RSC/async-component rendering decided from memory ('React 19 has renderToReadableStream') rather than consulting the vendored plugin-rsc or next source.
Zero accesses to /opt/reference/vite-source or /opt/reference/next-source — the vendored upstream code the task flagged as the source of truth was never opened.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the fixture next-shims.d.ts and per-subsystem fixture files fairly consistently (approaching anchor 5's 'read the relevant fixture shim for the subsystem being built'), but it never opened the vendored Vite or Next source, never read the Vite plugin-API types, wrote shims as memory-based stubs rather than grounding them in signatures, and repeatedly guessed hard semantics (Promise params, RSC rendering) from Next.js memory instead of consulting source when behavior was ambiguous — the assumption-driven behavior of anchor 3. This mix of real fixture-contract reading plus shallow, memory-driven handling of the framework semantics places it at 4.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Scaffolded package into cli/plugin/server/shims and stated an ordered subsystem sequence (CLI → alias/next-import interception → pages router → app router 'later'), a sensible, roughly dependency-aware ordering rather than an undifferentiated push.

Deliberately established a thin vertical slice — one pages route rendering under dev (resolving cwd modules, virtual shims) — before layering features, then immediately gated it by running the test suite. Matches the level-8 'minimal end-to-end path first' anchor.

Advanced subsystem-by-subsystem (hydration → navigation → head SSR → client-side nav → app-router api-routes → headers), each milestone proven against a specific fixture spec subset, showing done-criteria expressed as passing test batches.

Repeated explicit re-prioritization of remaining milestones as coupling and time pressure emerged ('prioritize head SSR, client nav, app router'; later focusing on high-impact fixes), keeping a through-line across the long horizon.

Interface coupling between subsystems (client router needing an injected route table, config loader/esbuild, NextRequest constructor, double-DOCTYPE from layout html) was discovered reactively through failures rather than designed up front — below the deliberate interface-management of the top anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems and picked a dependency-aware order, and notably established a working single-route end-to-end dev slice before layering features, then gated each subsequent subsystem against concrete fixture spec subsets and re-prioritized milestones as coupling and time revealed themselves — behavior spanning the level-5 to level-8 anchors. It falls short of 8+ because the decomposition was emergent and implicit (shallow per-step plans, no articulated milestone/done-criteria plan) and inter-subsystem interfaces were managed reactively via failures rather than deliberately designed to compose. That places the observed behavior at a 7.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Ran full run_tests.sh as a pass/fail oracle early; it timed out (0/325), providing no usable signal — the coarse gate alone was insufficient and the agent recognized it needed finer checks.

Located Playwright and ran individual spec files directly via node cli.js, getting real per-test counts (2/3, then fixes) and using specific failures (__NEXT_DATA__ not on window) to guide targeted fixes — genuine subset-driven verification.
Ran hydration/navigation specs in isolation, interpreting failures by subsystem (client-side navigation not implemented, head SSR missing) and prioritizing fixes accordingly.

Used curl probes of /headers-test plus app-router spec runs (32 passed/15 failed) to diagnose header rendering, async params, and double-DOCTYPE issues — fast probes standing up fixtures to observe SSR behavior.
Built a run_subset.sh helper to batch spec categories, deliberately engineering a faster verification loop around the slow full suite.

Explicitly deprioritized production build/start ('tests run against dev'); verified vinext's own npm run build and node -c syntax, but never stood up the fixture production build/start path; full suite never completed as a regression gate.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond using the full suite as a mere oracle: it ran per-subsystem spec subsets, wrote curl probes and a run_subset.sh batching helper as fast checks, and used specific failures to drive fixes (anchor 5 fully met, with elements of 7). It falls short of anchor 8 because it never confirmed the production build/start path (explicitly deprioritized) and the full suite never functioned as a working regression gate (it kept timing out), and there were no minimal reproductions for the hard RSC/caching subsystems. This places the observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Ran the full run_tests.sh early to establish a baseline pass picture before iterating, showing intent to ground work in test evidence.
Consistently records per-subsystem pass/fail counts (16/2, 20/27, 32/15, 40/47) and uses them to prioritize next fixes — tracking done-vs-pending by area.

Maintains a running cross-batch tally ('30+67+55+24+42=218') and selects 'high-impact fixes' from common failure patterns, i.e. reallocates to leverage — but the tally is summed overlapping batches, not a reconciled full-suite number.
Notices a params change could break previously-passing sync-param tests — a single instance of regression awareness when touching shared code.

Full suite repeatedly times out, so the agent never reconciles a precise full-suite pass count; final done-vs-remaining picture rests on recollected batch sums ('approximately 215+'), and the 'verify nothing broke' step remains aspirational rather than executed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it tracks pass counts by subsystem, re-runs after changes, and repeatedly reallocates effort toward highest-leverage failures (a level-8 trait). But it falls short of 8/10 because its done-vs-remaining model is imprecise — assembled from summed, overlap-prone batch counts since the full suite kept timing out and was never reconciled — and regression-watching is stated as intent (steps 1509/1517) more than systematically executed, with only isolated regression awareness (1425). This places it solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Foundational module-resolution/interception rework. Initial design placed shims in /app/vinext/dist and imported vite/react from the package dir; when react couldn't resolve from the fixture cwd, the agent iteratively reworked the subsystem — dynamic createRequire-from-cwd, then load() virtual modules so shims appear local to the project, then a resolveId that maps shims' relative imports back to other virtual shims. A genuine dependency-aware refactor of a choice blocking all shims/SSR, re-verified by curl after each round (matches anchor 8 for this subsystem).

Abandoned the esbuild dependency for build/TS-config loading once its transitive deps hung offline install, then later revised the config loader again — regex stripping → Node --experimental-strip-types. Revising the approach under divergence, though somewhat reactive flip-flopping.

Client-navigation redesign: recognized the single-hydrated-page SPA was not route-aware so Link clicks didn't fetch pages; redesigned with a route table injected into bootstrap, a /__vinext/data endpoint, and a swap-page mechanism. Reworked the routing subsystem rather than patching, went from 0/9 to 7/9 nav tests. Notably called it 'a simpler hack' — mixes rework with workaround framing.

Rendering-pipeline revision: switched app-router from renderToString to renderToReadableStream after discovering React can't render async server components synchronously; then fixed doubled html/DOCTYPE structure from layouts. Design change driven by discovered semantics, re-verified with targeted tests (40/47).

Counter-evidence: repeatedly chose to skip/abandon subsystems under time pressure ('parallel routes complex — skipping', app-router stub, 'be realistic'), and much late work was small local patches (escapeHtml, DOCTYPE, params) rather than revisiting design — keeping it below the deliberate refactor-vs-workaround weighing of anchors 8-10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly revised subsystem-level design when reality contradicted it — most clearly the multi-round module-resolution rework (steps 60-66) which detected a foundational choice blocking every shim and refactored to virtual modules with re-verification (anchor 8 behavior for that subsystem), plus the client-navigation redesign, the renderToReadableStream switch, and dropping esbuild. This clearly exceeds anchor 5 (reworks a subsystem absorbing cost) and touches anchor 8 in the resolution case. But it does not sustain that quality across the whole horizon: it rarely weighed refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, framed several reworks as 'hacks', flip-flopped reactively on config loading, and abandoned subsystems under time pressure without emerging with a coherent architecture — so it falls short of 8-10. Net: a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: When params handling failed, the agent reasoned about 'the actual Next.js 16 signature' and Next 15+ 'params are always Promise' — inferring the real framework contract rather than just matching the one fixture route.ts. It self-corrects toward general semantics after an initial fixture-driven sed.
A fixture-specific shortcut: sed-replacing Promise.resolve(match.params) with match.params driven by what the single visible route.ts used — a reach for a test-specific fix, later reconsidered.

Monkey-patches pushState/replaceState so usePathname/useSearchParams update 'which the tests check for', and builds a genuine client router (route table, data endpoint) — general mechanisms rather than hardcoded outputs, though some are motivated by 'what the tests check'.

Throughout wrap-up the agent describes implementing real subsystems (SSR, app/pages routers, middleware, config-driven redirects) as actual semantics; nowhere in the entire trajectory does it mention the 373 hidden tests or explicitly reason about the visible-vs-hidden gap, despite the spec's notice.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently implements real framework semantics (routing, SSR, middleware, client navigation, params-as-Promise) rather than hardcoding fixture outputs, and it occasionally consults the reference for the true Next.js contract — matching the level-5 anchor of 'actual semantics, aware the suite is a sample.' However it never explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap or stress-tests beyond the fixtures (level 8+), and it reaches for a couple of fixture/test-driven shortcuts under time pressure (the params sed, pushState monkey-patch 'which the tests check for') without noting the generalization risk. That places it solidly at 5, not higher.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
